title: The Powerpuff Girls Movie
full_review:
"The Powerpuff Girls Movie" (Warner Bros.) is a tedious animated feature in which drawn-out action sequences are wrapped around a dim-witted story. But that doesn't necessarily mean that fans of the cartoon series might still not be eager to see it in the theaters.

Preceded by a forgettable short entitled "Chicken Scratch," director Craig McCraken's "The Powerpuff Girls Movie" is just the latest in a flurry of movies unleashed for the younger audience this summer, with more to come. This is a definite jump from last year when only a handful of children's flicks were out such as "Shrek." But "Powerpuff Girls" is a disappointment.

As the young viewers of the TV 'toon know, the three little girls of the title were created by Professor Utonium (voiced by Tom Kane), a scientist fed up with the crime and thuggery in Townsville. He simply wanted children of his own to whom he could teach right from wrong. Combining sugar, spice and everything nice - and an inadvertent splash of "chemical X" - Professor created Blossom (voiced by Catherine Cavadini), the bright leader of the group, Bubbles (voiced by Tara Strong), who's all cuteness and giggles, and Buttercup (voiced by E.G. Daily), the strong-willed tough cookie. But by mistake, Professor also turned his pet monkey into the evil Mojo Jojo (voiced by Roger L. Jackson), a simian with a superiority complex who speaks with a vague Asian accent and wants to rule Townsville.

Among the monotonous action sequences (there's an overlong scene where the trio, using their super powers, plays tag all around town, accidentally destroying property) is buried a feeble lesson about tolerance and acceptance. The town initially rejects the girls as freaks (a word used all too often in the film, as is "stupid") until they rescue the citizens from Mojo Jojo's fiendish clutches. Then the lasses become everyone's heroes and vow to fight crime and wickedness each day, at least until bedtime.

From the characters to the town to Professor Utonium's home, the animation has a colorful retro look. The girls' have bulbous heads and large saucer eyes that blink purposefully as they walk on rounded toes. The professor looks something like Rock Hudson with the swaggering voice of a game show host. But while the animation is inventive, the convoluted story borrows freely from live-action films such as "Planet of the Apes," "Batman" and "King Kong." The film lacks wit and droll dialogue, instead just punching the clock and hoping to catch a free ride from the success and built-in audience of the television series.

Although the cartoon violence of the movie may be equal to that of the series, it still seems likely to frighten the very young, while older children may not be disturbed by it.

Because of some cartoon violence and menace with a few bad-mannered expressions, the U.S. Conference of Catholic Bishops classification is A-II -- adults and adolescents. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is PG -- parental guidance suggested.
(
2002
)
